newsitem.title: GERMANY: German expellees still angry at Czech pact.
newsitem.headline: German expellees still angry at Czech pact.

text.p: Around 100,000 ethnic Germans expelled from Czech lands after World War Two used a turbulent weekend congress to vent their anger at a German-Czech reconciliation pact which they say has betrayed them.

The so-called "Sudeten Germans" and their descendants booed and whistled loudly at Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber, both leaders of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) which has been the group's patron.

Earlier this year Bonn and Prague sealed an accord intended to heal resentment left over from the war, when Nazi Germany occupied then-Czechoslovakia and the Czechs subsequently drove out more than two million ethnic Germans branded as traitors.

The pact included bilateral projects to improve relations and allocated funds to compensate Czech victims of the occupation, but provided no hope that Prague might one day return property to expropriated ethnic Germans.

The Sudeten Germans' leader, Franz Neubauer, said the cause of reconciliation had been harmed by the fact that the Sudeten Germans were not allowed to take part in negotiating the pact, and by Prague's refusal to declare the expulsions a crime.

"No one can expect the Sudeten Germans to follow the foreign ministers of both countries like lemmings into the dead end that they call the road to the future," he told the group's annual congress held in Nuremberg.
Stoiber, whose southeastern state of Bavaria took in most of the Sudeten Germans, urged the expellees to "make use of this chance and not stand on the sidelines".
But he also insisted that the Czechs formally give the Sudeten Germans the right to take up residence again in their homeland.

Waigel, who sparked a row when he demanded at last year's Sudeten congress that Prague respect the rule of law by declaring the expulsions illegal, was also loudly booed as he addressed the congress on Saturday.
He was heckled as he said Nazism had inflicted untold suffering on the Czech people, and that the bilateral accord was a pragmatic solution.
But he also urged the Czech side to seek dialogue with the Sudeten Germans and not try to dilute the terms of the accord.
